newsitem.title: FRANCE: Far-right playing decisive role in French election.
newsitem.headline: Far-right playing decisive role in French election.

text.p: French far-right leader Jean-Marie Le Pen and his National Front are savouring the possibility of winning up to three National Assembly seats and playing a decisive role in the parliamentary election runoff on June 1.

In Sundays first round, according to voter surveys, the Front won between 14.8 and 15.3 percent, well above its 12.4 percent score in 1993 and possibly higher than the 15 percent Le Pen took in the 1995 presidential election.
The polls projected that, after the second round vote, the xenophobic party would hold as many as three seats in the new National Assembly, where it now has none,
The vote means the Front is within reach of a parliamentary platform to give its ideas greater public prominence.
The Front "has won a very great victory this evening", Le Pen told supporters in a televised statement.
"I urge all voters...to massively mobilise next Sunday so that the National Front can elect enough deputies to enable the voice of France to be heard."
Le Pen also declared that the result showed conservative President Jacques Chirac had failed and urged him to resign.
"President Chirac injected himself personally into the battle. He is defeated, he must leave," he said.

The Front, which espouses racial inequality, backs a constitutional preference for "native-born" French people in jobs and state benefits and wants to ship home even legal immigrants, has been in the past primarily a party of protest, a magnet for voters dissatisfied with mainstream politics.

But this year, pollsters predict a close contest with Front voters possibly deciding the final outcome -- though perhaps not in the way intended by Le Pen, who has urged voters to "zap" the governing centre-right coalition from power.

Voter surveys show Front supporters could hold the key to the final result, their decision to back either government candidates or leftists in the second round being capable of swinging the race either way.

The presence of Front candidates in many three-way runoffs will in any case enable Le Pen to keep up his vitriolic attacks on Chirac and put new pressure on the majority to cut a political deal in exchange for his support.
The Front has been riding high since winning control of a fourth municipality in February, pressuring the centre-right government into beefing up France's already tight immigration laws.

The fourth city hall was in Vitrolles, won by Catherine Megret, wife of Front number two Bruno Megret, who was ineligible to run. The other city halls in National Front hands are in Marignane, Orange and Toulon.
But it has not been an easy campaign for Le Pen, who at 68 insists he is giving no thought to retiring as party leader.
Though a candidate in past general elections, Le Pen did not stand this year, prompting critics to say he feared losing and raising questions within the party about his future role.
Top deputies Megret and Bruno Gollnisch are both standing in the election and have been openly manoeuvring to succeed him if and when he steps down.
Other Front candidates who might win seats are Toulon mayor Jean-Marie Le Chevallier and Orange mayor Jacques Bompard.
Questions about Le Pen's future took on greater prominence after some Front loyalists questioned his statements that a leftist win would be preferable to a government victory.
Le Pen said that power-sharing between Chirac and the left would derail the president's drive for European integration, which Le Pen has described as "Hitler's dream come true".
